opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the main goal was to change how people *feel* about agents, not just how they think about them. Everyone on the team reads papers and benchmarks, and it's easy to form an abstract picture: "agents are getting better, long-horizon tasks are the next frontier." But that picture stays abstract until you actually hand real work to one and watch what happens.

So I asked everyone, researchers, engineers, even people on the data side, to use it seriously in their daily workflow for a while. Not as a demo, but for the actual things they had to get done. I wanted a few things out of that.

First, to build intuition about where the real gaps are. When you use it yourself, you notice very quickly that the failures aren't always where the benchmarks say they are. Sometimes the model is smart enough but loses track of context over a long session, or it's too eager and doesn't know when to stop and ask. Those details matter a lot for how we design training data and RL environments, and you only really feel them through hands-on use.

Second, I wanted people to experience the shift in how work gets done. Once you've had an agent run for an hour on something and come back with a reasonable result, your sense of what a model *should* be changes. You stop thinking of it as a chatbot that answers questions and start thinking of it as something that takes on tasks. That changes what you prioritize when you train your own models.

And third, honestly, it was about urgency. Seeing firsthand what the best systems can already do makes it very clear how far we still need to go, and how fast the field is moving. I think that kind of direct experience motivates people more than any slide I could show them.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest's response directly, without tools.

Honestly, it started from a kind of anxiety. I had this feeling that the way we build models and the way people actually use them were drifting apart. We spend all day looking at benchmarks, loss curves, eval numbers, and those tell you something, but they don't tell you what it feels like to hand an agent a real task and watch where it stumbles.

So I asked everyone, not just the researchers but the infra people, the product people, even folks who don't write much code, to spend real time with OpenClaude on their actual work. Not a demo, not a toy problem. Your real work. Let it touch your codebase, let it handle something annoying you've been putting off.

A few things I wanted out of that. First, intuition. You can't design good training objectives for agentic behavior if you've never felt the frustration of an agent that confidently does the wrong thing for twenty minutes. Those moments teach you more than a hundred eval cases. Second, I wanted to collapse the distance between "model team" and "user." When your own engineers are the first and most demanding users, the feedback loop gets very tight and very honest. People complain to you in the hallway. That's valuable.

And third, frankly, I wanted to change the culture a bit. There was still a mindset of "the model is the product, the agent layer is someone else's problem." I don't believe that anymore. The scaffolding, the tool use, the way the system recovers from mistakes, those are now inseparable from what the model is. If the team doesn't live inside that experience, we'll optimize the wrong things.

What surprised me was how quickly people's priorities shifted. Within a couple of weeks, the questions in our meetings changed. Less "how do we gain two points on this benchmark," more "why does it lose track of the goal after the fifth step" or "why doesn't it ask when it's clearly uncertain." Those are the right questions. That was really the whole point.
